adventure.name: Josric Pickle's Practical Course for Adventurers

contents.name: Josric Pickle's Practical Course for Adventurers

data.name: Josric Pickle's Practical Course for Adventurers

entries.name: Adventure Guide
entries: A 2024-rules one-shot for 3–6 3rd-level characters, built for a roughly three-hour Hall of Heroes session. The baseline assumes experienced, creative players using maximum hit points and spending resources aggressively because this is a one-shot.

The adventure is intentionally linear at the room level but permissive inside each challenge. Players should be rewarded for bypassing, reframing, smashing, talking through, or otherwise solving a room in a way Josric did not anticipate.
All library chambers are separate spaces in-world but look almost exactly alike. Reuse the same physical room layout. The repetition is part of the premise, not a convenience.

entries.name: Background
entries: Josric Pickle was once the most accomplished student at his magical school and was especially fond of designing puzzles. He proposed a practical training course for adventurers, but his peers laughed at the idea. Josric decided to prove that the course worked.

He hires the characters to recover his supposedly stolen spellbook and tells them to meet him at his library. The spellbook was never stolen. The job, the library, and the dangers inside are all parts of Josric's practical examination.
Josric is proud, theatrical, and sincere about the value of the course. He wants to be proven right, not to kill anyone.

The repeated rooms should feel increasingly strange. Each north door leads to another library chamber with the same dimensions, shelves, fireplace, tables, and exits. The south door behind the party no longer opens once they enter a lesson room.

entries.caption: Josric at a Glance
rows: About 5'9", lean and slightly narrow-shouldered, with the restless posture of someone whose mind is always a few steps ahead of the conversation.
Silver-brown hair, thinning slightly at the crown and never quite lying flat; short, neatly trimmed beard with more silver than brown.
Hazel, usually bright with amusement or concentration; he wears small round brass-framed spectacles when reading or inspecting something closely.

A well-made burgundy academic coat cut like formal wizard's robes but worn over a charcoal waistcoat, cream shirt, dark trousers, and practical black boots. The coat has too many inner pockets, several of them holding chalk, folded notes, bits of string, or small puzzle pieces. His clothes are expensive enough to show that he has done well for himself, but practical enough that he actually uses them.
Ink-stained fingertips and a faint chalk smudge somewhere on one sleeve more often than not.
A successful academic who is trying very hard to look dignified while being visibly delighted that someone is finally participating in the thing he has wanted to prove for years.

entries.name: Voice
entries: Use a warm, precise, professorial voice with crisp diction and a slightly theatrical rhythm. Josric sounds like a teacher who has rehearsed the lesson in his head and has been waiting far too long for someone to take the class.
At rest, speak at a measured pace and keep him controlled. When a player does something clever, let the voice speed up and brighten because Josric is genuinely excited by good problem-solving.
For lesson announcements, give him a little extra projection and deliberate emphasis, as though he is presenting to a lecture hall even when only four people are standing in front of him.
He should sound smug sometimes, but not sinister. The important undercurrent is enthusiasm: Josric wants the course to work and is thrilled when the adventurers surprise him.
His laugh is usually a short, satisfied 'Ha!' rather than a long cackle.

entries.name: Roleplaying Josric
entries: Josric likes explaining why something was educational after the characters have already survived it.
He does not mock failure cruelly. A mistake interests him because it tells him something about the course.
When the players bypass one of his intended solutions, his first reaction is usually a flash of annoyance followed almost immediately by fascination.
He is proud enough to want credit for the course, but intellectually honest enough to recognize when the adventurers have improved his design by breaking it.

entries.name: Running the Three-Hour Session

entries.caption: Flexible Session Clock
rows: Character introductions, Josric's job, arrival at the library.
Reveal, payment, closing beat. Finishing 20–30 minutes early is acceptable.

entries: Do not stretch a solved room merely to fill time. If a sharp table finishes early, let them finish early.

entries.name: Optional-Room Pacing
entries: Behind schedule: skip both optional rooms and go directly from the Unlocked Door to the Mirror Gallery.
On pace: run either the Librarian or two Teamwork door pairs.
Ahead: run the Librarian plus two or three Teamwork door pairs.
Far ahead: run the Librarian and all four Teamwork door pairs.

entries.name: Physical Table Setup
entries: This section is intentionally specific to the terrain available for this table. The Designer's Notes for Grayson stay equipment-agnostic so the adventure can still make sense years from now with different terrain.

items: Use the Melee Mats 22×26 grid as the floor.
Use both STAHLHAMMERS Dungeon Walls sets for the repeated stone perimeter, room dividers, and door-wall pieces.
Use the AUSPDICE library set as the repeated visual anchor: 3 large bookcases and 2 small cabinets. Keep their relative positions as consistent as practical from room to room.
Use the AF634A tavern furniture as library furniture where useful: fireplace, round reading table and chairs, cabinets/shelving, and the L-shaped bar as the Librarian's circulation desk.
Use the existing chest pieces as the physical revealed forms of Book Mimics.
Use paper/card mirror standees in acrylic bases for the Mirror Gallery. Match each mirror to its Echo with the same numbered blank condition ring.
Keep the center lanes open enough for 3–6 PCs to move. The visual repetition matters more than reproducing every square of the setup maps exactly.

entries.name: Opening: Find the Stolen Spellbook

entries: Josric Pickle hired the characters to recover his stolen spellbook and asked them to meet him at his private library.
Josric is not waiting for them. A note in his hand is left where they will immediately find it.
I may have found another lead and have gone to follow it. Begin without me. Search the library thoroughly. If my spellbook is here, find it. — Josric Pickle
There is no thief. Josric wrote the note to get the characters moving through the course without explaining what the library really is.
The first chamber looks like an ordinary private library. Once the entire party enters, the south door closes and will not reopen.
When the characters pass through the north door, the next chamber looks almost exactly the same. Do not explain the repetition. Let the players discover the premise through play.

entries.name: Room 1: Book Mimics
Terrain Setup
entries: Build the standard repeated library with the 3 large AUSPDICE bookcases, 2 small cabinets, fireplace, reading furniture, and north/south STAHLHAMMERS door-walls.
Do not place obvious monsters at setup. When the Mimics reveal themselves, use chest pieces as their table representations.
For 3–5 Mimics, spread the revealed chest pieces around the shelves without blocking every central movement lane.
The first lesson is an easy combat about awareness, not attrition.

A character who deliberately examines the books before touching or disturbing them can notice signs such as a faintly flexing cover, damp page edges, or a leather binding that seems to breathe. If a check is needed, use a moderate Wisdom (Perception) check; DC 13 is a suggested table default rather than a required canon number.
If the party notices and reacts before the attack, they avoid the ambush. Otherwise, apply the 2024 Surprise procedure when initiative begins.
Use {@creature Book Mimic|JPTC2026}. Their purpose is to cling, move, and make the environment feel dangerous without draining the party before the rest of the course.
Excellent! Lesson One complete. A surprising number of adventurers die because they fail to notice that the furniture is breathing.
The lesson is: {@b A good adventurer pays attention to their surroundings.}
When the room is cleared, the first required Lesson Marker appears: {@b JOSRIC PICKLE}.
The north door opens.

entries.name: Room 2: See, Think, Act
Terrain Setup
entries: Use the standard repeated library layout.
Treat the north large bookcase as the puzzle shelf. Six paper/book markers can identify the Eye, Sword, Hand, Head, Foot, and Heart without adding new furniture.
Keep the north door physically in its normal location; it remains sealed until the room is solved.
The exit is sealed. Above the prominent puzzle shelf are three words: {@b SEE. THINK. ACT.}
Six distinctive books are displayed with large symbols on their spines: an Eye, a Sword, a Hand, a Head, a Foot, and a Heart.
The intended solution is intentionally simple: {@b Eye → Head → Hand}. Eye means SEE, Head means THINK, and Hand means ACT.
A wrong choice causes a harmless magical response and resets the sequence. Use funny or curious effects—a bell, a puff of dust, a book briefly scolding the character—rather than damage.

Investigation, Arcana, Detect Magic, Mage Hand, tools, physical experimentation, or another sensible method can reveal or bypass parts of the puzzle. Reward workable solutions instead of protecting the intended sequence.
If the table has been genuinely stuck for about 7–8 minutes, let Josric's magic provide a small hint rather than allowing the room to become a bottleneck.
The lesson is: {@b A good adventurer uses more than weapons to succeed.}
When solved, the second required Lesson Marker appears: {@b YOUR STUDENTS}.
The north door opens.

entries.name: Room 3: The Unlocked Door
Terrain Setup
entries: Use the standard repeated library.
Use the normal north STAHLHAMMERS door-wall. The absurd reinforcement is mainly descriptive; a removable paper/card overlay can make it visually distinct without needing a special terrain piece.
Use one or more chest/cabinet pieces as plausible places for the useless keys.

Everything in the library is normal except the north door. Describe it in unreasonable detail: thick reinforced steel, heavy hinges, numerous keyholes, deadbolts, combination mechanisms, and arcane-looking etchings.
The room contains clues leading to keys. The keys do not open the door because the door is not locked.
Picking or manipulating the visible locks is extraordinarily difficult. Even a successful attempt can produce a satisfying click without changing the actual state of the door.
Any character who simply turns the handle opens the door. No roll.
Do not make the room harder because the players solve it quickly. If someone tries the handle immediately, the room can last seconds.
The lesson is exactly: {@b Problems are not always as complicated as they seem.}
When the door opens, the third required Lesson Marker appears: {@b AWAIT}.

entries.name: Optional Room: The Librarian
Terrain Setup
entries: Use the standard repeated library.
Use the AF634A L-shaped bar as the circulation/reference desk.
Place the Librarian behind the desk and keep the north door in its usual position.
This room is optional and exists as a pacing reserve. Skip it when the session is running long; use it when the group is ahead.
A magical Librarian blocks passage and states that the party is not authorized to enter the restricted collection.
The Librarian cares about authorization, order, and protecting the collection. The simplest solution is Josric's original note, which counts as adequate authorization.

Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, exploiting bureaucracy, forged credentials, or another plausible social approach can work. Do not roll when the evidence or argument obviously satisfies what the Librarian wants. If a roll is useful, DC 13 is a suggested default; DC 15 is appropriate only for a thin or risky argument.
If attacked, a magical barrier simply prevents the attack from reaching the Librarian.
Violence is not an accepted form of identification.
The lesson is exactly: {@b A good adventurer learns what someone wants before deciding what to say.}
This optional room contains no required Lesson Marker.

entries.name: Optional Room: The Teamwork Doors
Terrain Setup
entries: Use pieces from both STAHLHAMMERS wall sets to divide the repeated library into two parallel lanes.
Place only one active door-wall at the far end of each lane. Keep the remaining door-wall pieces off the board as reserve pairs.
Use the library shelves and selected tavern cabinets/tables as lane dressing and as physical homes for the current mechanisms.
After a pair is solved, either end the room or place the next door pair beyond the current threshold. The players should never see the total number of prepared pairs.
This room is optional, just like the Librarian. It is a pacing control: skip it when the session is running long, or use it when the party is ahead.
Split the party as evenly as practical. The groups can hear one another but cannot cross the center divider.
Core rule: {@b no group can open its own current door. Interacting with one side releases the opposite side's door.}

entries.caption: Prepared Door Pairs
rows: Picking, manipulating, or breaking the physical lock releases Side B. Arcana, Knock, dispelling, or another magical interaction with the seal releases Side A.
Pulling or forcing the lever releases Side B. Precision work on the latch releases Side A.
Each side has information needed to operate the other side's controls; they must communicate, then reverse roles.
Both groups must coordinate and operate their mechanisms at the same agreed moment.

entries: The hidden accordion can contain 2–4 door pairs. If the first pair takes about ten minutes, run only two total. If the party is fast, use three or four.
Do not require a Rogue, Wizard, strong character, or any specific class. Clever substitutions work.
The lesson is: {@b Some problems can only be solved by working together.}
This optional room contains no required Lesson Marker.

entries.name: Room 4: The Mirror Gallery
Terrain Setup
entries: Use the standard repeated library.
Place one paper/card mirror standee in an acrylic base for each PC. Put a numbered blank condition ring on each mirror base and the matching number on its Echo.
Spread the mirrors through the open floor around the repeated shelves so both the Echoes and their source mirrors are tactically reachable.
One standing mirror appears for each PC. Each mirror produces an Echo that looks exactly like that character but uses a simple prebuilt class-themed monster card rather than a copied character sheet.
Use one Echo per PC. Species traits and background details are visual only.
For a multiclass PC, use the class with more levels; on a tie, use the class listed first.
Each Echo is linked to one physical mirror.

entries.name: Standing Mirror
entries: {@b Armor Class} 11
{@b Hit Points} 10
{@b Speed} 0 ft.
{@b Damage Vulnerability} bludgeoning
The mirror has no actions. When reduced to 0 hit points, its linked Echo immediately shatters and is destroyed.
Destroying a mirror immediately destroys its linked Echo. This is an intended solution, not an exploit.
Echoes never attack unconscious PCs.
The lesson is: {@b Sometimes you are your own worst enemy.}
When the room is cleared, the fourth required Lesson Marker appears: {@b THE FINAL LESSON}.
The north door opens.

entries.name: Emergency Recovery
entries: Immediately after the Mirror Gallery and before the final room, the course presents an obviously benevolent recovery fixture.
A lesson ends when something is learned, not when the student can no longer stand.

Each character can use it once. If below 75 percent of maximum hit points, the character regains enough hit points to reach 75 percent of maximum, rounded up. If at 0 hit points, the character becomes conscious before this healing is applied.
The fixture also ends ordinary conditions created by the course that would otherwise carry into the finale.
It does not restore spell slots, Rage, Action Surge, Bardic Inspiration, Channel Divinity, consumables, or other major class resources.
This is core infrastructure, not an optional reward.

entries.name: Final Room: Find His Book
Terrain Setup
entries: Use the standard repeated library.
Place the AF634A round reading table or another reading table at the center as the spellbook stand. Put a visible spellbook marker on it.
Keep Josric and all staged finale creatures off the board until the summoning phrase is spoken.
The room is quiet. Josric's spellbook sits openly on the central table. Josric is nowhere in sight.
The four required Lesson Markers read: {@b JOSRIC PICKLE / YOUR STUDENTS / AWAIT / THE FINAL LESSON}.
Together they form the summoning phrase: {@b 'Josric Pickle, your students await the final lesson.'}
Speaking that phrase—or a clearly equivalent statement that shows the party has understood it—summons Josric.
The optional Librarian and Teamwork rooms never contain required pieces of the phrase.
If a required marker was missed, the spellbook itself supplies enough context to reconstruct the missing words. Do not turn the summoning phrase into another difficult puzzle.
Josric appears, reveals that there was never a theft, congratulates the party for reaching the end of his Practical Course for Adventurers, and announces the final examination.

entries.name: When Josric Appears

entries: A lean human man in his late fifties appears beside the spellbook in a flicker of pale arcane light. Silver-brown hair refuses to stay neatly combed above a pair of round brass spectacles. His burgundy academic coat is immaculate at first glance, until you notice the ink on his fingertips, the chalk on one sleeve, and the collection of small objects bulging from too many pockets. He looks over the room, then over all of you, with the unmistakable expression of a professor whose favorite experiment has just produced a very interesting result.
Josric smiles, straightens his coat, and addresses the party in his warm, precise lecture-hall voice.

entries.name: Final Exam: Josric Pickle
entries: Use {@creature Josric Pickle|JPTC2026}. His defensive chassis is the published 2024 Mage, using maximum hit points, with offense deliberately reduced for a level-3 training fight.

Before the session, choose up to three prepared Josric Reflection class cards and put them in the initiative tracker in the order you want them to appear. Do not invent Reflection abilities at the table.
The listed later waves are the maximum planned pressure, not a promise. If the party is already struggling, hold back a later Mimic or Reflection wave. The players never know how many were prepared.
Do not increase Josric's hit points, AC, attack bonus, or damage in the middle of the fight.
Josric makes two Arcane Burst attacks with his action and normally splits them between different conscious targets when possible.
The Book Mimics are nuisances and positioning pressure. The Reflections create different tactical problems. Josric remains the actual objective.
{@b Victory condition: defeat Josric.} The instant Josric reaches 0 hit points or yields, every remaining Reflection shatters, every course creature stops attacking, and the exam ends.

entries.name: Josric Tactics
entries: Use Shield or Counterspell through Protective Magic when it meaningfully changes the fight.
Use Misty Step if Josric is surrounded, pinned, or needs to reposition.
Do not use dangerous Mage area-damage spells in this examination.
Do not attack unconscious PCs.
If the fight is clearly decided, Josric can yield instead of forcing the party to grind through the last hit points.
The final lesson is exactly: {@b A good adventurer knows when to use everything they've learned.}
Knowing something is useful. Knowing when to use it makes you an adventurer.

entries.name: Mirror Echo Quick Reference
entries: For an unfamiliar third-party class, choose the fallback that most closely matches its obvious combat role. This is the only at-table judgment call required for an unprepared class.

entries.caption: Published Chassis Reference
rows: Barbarian / Fighter / Paladin / Brute / Blood Hunter
Simple armored or melee baseline, then apply the printed Echo tweak.
Wizard / Sorcerer / Warlock / Artificer / Druid / Caster

entries: The Echo cards in this file are the initiative-ready reskins/tweaks. The chassis note preserves the design rule: published stat block first, small clear modification second.

entries.name: Resolution and Rewards
entries: When Josric is defeated, the course stops immediately. He is winded, annoyed if they exploited something he did not anticipate, and delighted that the course produced exactly the kind of adaptive behavior he wanted to prove was valuable.
Josric admits that the spellbook was never stolen. He hired them because he needed real adventurers to test the course rather than classmates who already knew his habits.

He pays the agreed contract fee. For a standalone Hall one-shot, the exact gold amount can be whatever the table normally uses; the important reward is the completed course and Josric's acknowledgment that the party proved his peers wrong.
If the group failed the final exam, Josric still releases them, treats injuries, and explains which lessons they mastered. Failure should end the test, not the characters.

entries.caption: Room Lessons and Summoning Marks
rows: A good adventurer pays attention to their surroundings.
A good adventurer uses more than weapons to succeed.
Problems are not always as complicated as they seem.
A good adventurer learns what someone wants before deciding what to say.
Some problems can only be solved by working together.
Sometimes you are your own worst enemy.
A good adventurer knows when to use everything they've learned.

items: All PCs are level 3; balance assumptions use maximum HP and aggressive one-shot resource use.
Book Mimics: maximum-HP Juvenile Mimic chassis plus normal Mimic Adhesive behavior.
Optional rooms: Librarian and Teamwork. Skip one or both when running long.
Teamwork accordion: 2–4 hidden door pairs; players never know the total.
Mirror Gallery: one Echo per PC; standing mirrors are AC 11, HP 10, speed 0, vulnerable to bludgeoning; destroying a mirror destroys its Echo.
Recovery raises badly hurt PCs to 75 percent HP and does not restore major class resources.
Required phrase: 'Josric Pickle, your students await the final lesson.'
Josric: AC 15, 144 HP, two Arcane Bursts, Misty Step 3/day, Protective Magic 3/day (Shield or Counterspell).
Josric normally splits his two Arcane Bursts between different conscious targets.
Later finale waves can be held back if the party is already struggling.
Defeating or forcing Josric to yield immediately ends the exam.
Do not add filler if the party is fast. Finishing early is acceptable.
Reward plausible unexpected solutions. The course is about adaptation.

entries.name: Josric in 10 Seconds
entries: Human, 58; lean; silver-brown hair and short beard; round brass spectacles; burgundy academic coat over practical dark clothes; ink-stained fingers.
Voice: warm, precise, professorial, mildly theatrical; speeds up when excited; smug but never sinister.
Core attitude: 'I knew this course would work, and you just proved it—possibly in a way I did not plan for.'

entries.name: Where I Started
entries: When I started thinking about this one-shot, I had three different ideas in my head. One was a Battle of the Bands adventure. One was a dungeon that turned out to be a game show. The idea that stuck was the strangest and simplest: a room you cannot seem to leave.

The feeling was loosely inspired by Cube. I was interested in the disorientation of moving forward, opening another door, and finding a space that seems impossibly familiar. I was not trying to copy Cube's traps or story.
That became the central visual idea: the characters are moving through different rooms, but every room has been deliberately built to look almost exactly the same.
The library followed naturally. Books, shelves, hidden information, Mimics, puzzles, mirrors, and a missing spellbook all fit together.

entries.name: From Thomage to Josric Pickle
entries: My first name for the wizard was Thomage. That name came out of my own head very early while I was still figuring out what the adventure was.
The rooms actually came before most of his story. Once the course started taking shape, I needed a reason somebody would build something like this.

I decided he had been the most accomplished student at his magical school, loved designing puzzles, and proposed a practical course for adventurers. His peers laughed at the idea, so he built the course to prove that it worked.
Later I changed Thomage to Josric Pickle. I wanted the name to feel a little closer to mine, and I liked the joke that the adventurers were literally in a pickle.
The spellbook theft became his lie. Nobody stole it. It was sitting at the end of the course the entire time.

entries.name: The Rule That Started Guiding Everything
entries: The biggest design rule I found while making this was that I did not want rooms with one protected answer.
I wanted to give the players a problem and then respect a reasonable solution even if it was not the one I expected.

If somebody immediately tries the unlocked door, it opens. If somebody destroys a mirror instead of fighting the Echo, the Echo dies. If somebody shows the Librarian the authorization they already have, that works. If somebody finds a better solution to the book puzzle, I should let it work.
The adventure became better every time I stopped protecting my answer.

entries.name: Room 1: Book Mimics
entries: I wanted the first room to be simple combat, but I wanted it to teach something immediately.
The lesson became awareness. The danger is sitting in the room pretending to be harmless, and paying attention can prevent the ambush.
The published Juvenile Mimic was a better starting point than a full Mimic because this fight is supposed to be memorable and funny, not nearly kill the party in the first room.
I used the maximum hit points from the Juvenile Mimic chassis and added the normal Mimic's Adhesive behavior because I specifically liked the image of books latching onto adventurers.

entries.name: Room 2: The Book Puzzle
entries: I wanted a room that could not be solved by just attacking it. The lesson became that a good adventurer uses more than weapons.
I was initially worried that a puzzle needed to be difficult to be worthwhile. I eventually went the other direction.
SEE, THINK, ACT—Eye, Head, Hand—is intentionally simple. The fun is in noticing it, experimenting, using skills or spells, or doing something I did not predict.
Wrong answers are harmless because I do not want to teach the players that experimentation is something they should avoid.

entries.name: The Room I Cut
entries: At one point I wanted a room built around the lesson 'learn from the past.'
I liked the lesson more than any version of the room I could make.
The idea involved records of failed adventurers and learning from the mistakes of people who had gone through before. Every version became too complicated compared with the rest of the course.
So I cut it instead of forcing it to stay.
I am leaving the idea in the archive on purpose.
Grayson: I never solved the 'learn from the past' room to my satisfaction. Maybe you will.

entries.name: Room 3: The Unlocked Door
entries: The history room was replaced by one of the simplest ideas in the whole adventure.
I make the exit look absurdly secure: reinforced door, locks, keyholes, wards, keys hidden around the room, everything telling the players that this is going to be difficult.
The door is not locked.
If somebody tries the handle immediately, the room can be over in seconds. I do not want to punish them for solving it quickly. That is the room working.
The lesson is exactly what happens: problems are not always as complicated as they seem.

entries.name: The Optional Librarian
entries: I realized I had combat, observation, and puzzles, but I did not yet have a room built around talking to somebody.

The Librarian wants authorization. The party already has a perfectly good piece of authorization in Josric's note, but persuasion, deception, intimidation, bureaucracy, or another sensible social solution can work.
The real lesson is not simply 'talk your way through it.' It is learning what somebody wants before deciding what to say.
I made this room optional because it also gives me control over a three-hour session. If the group is running long, I skip it. If they are ahead, I use it.

entries.name: The Optional Teamwork Room
entries: The first version of the teamwork room got too complicated. I kept adding moving shelves, controls, mechanisms, and other pieces until the machinery was taking over the idea.
The part I actually cared about was simple: split the party into two groups, let them communicate, and make each group responsible for opening the other group's door.
That became a hidden accordion of two to four door pairs. The players never know how many pairs exist.
This room is optional too, just like the Librarian. If I am running long, I skip it. If I need a little more adventure, I use one or two pairs. If the group is flying, I can use three or four.
The lesson is that some problems can only be solved by working together.

entries.name: Room 4: The Mirror Gallery
entries: Fighting versions of the characters was one of the ideas I wanted very early.
I did not want to copy whole character sheets because that would make the room miserable to run. I built simple class-themed Echoes instead.
I also prepared Artificer, Blood Hunter, and generic role cards so I would not be inventing an enemy while everybody waited at the table.
The first versions of the Echoes were too durable in simulated playtesting. Then I realized that a player was obviously going to attack the mirror.
Instead of preventing that, I made the mirror the source. Destroy the mirror and its Echo shatters.
That made the room much better because understanding the source of the problem becomes just as valid as winning a straight fight.

entries.name: Why I Added the Recovery Station
entries: I did not want unlucky damage in an earlier room to turn the final fight into a cleanup exercise.
I also did not want a full rest to erase every resource decision from the course.
So the recovery station restores badly hurt characters to about three-quarters of their hit points without restoring their major class resources.
That keeps the earlier rooms meaningful and makes sense for Josric. He built a training course, not a death trap.

entries.name: The Lesson Markers
entries: I wanted the rooms to connect to the ending, so the four required lessons leave the phrase JOSRIC PICKLE / YOUR STUDENTS / AWAIT / THE FINAL LESSON.
The phrase is 'Josric Pickle, your students await the final lesson.'
The optional rooms are not required for this. I did not want pacing-control rooms to become mandatory because of a missing clue.
If a required marker gets missed, the spellbook at the end gives enough context to reconstruct it. The phrase is a payoff, not another bottleneck.

entries.name: Designing Josric's Final Fight
entries: The Hall players I expect to run this for are not a good match for ordinary encounter assumptions. They have maximum hit points, they know how to use their characters, and in a one-shot they have no reason to save resources for tomorrow.

That made me care less about a neat Challenge Rating and more about two practical questions: can Josric survive focused attacks long enough to feel like a boss, and can he do it without deleting a level-three character in one turn?
I settled on the published 2024 Mage as the defensive chassis and used the maximum possible hit points from its Hit Dice: 144.
I kept Misty Step and Protective Magic, but reduced the offense to two Arcane Bursts instead of three and excluded the dangerous area-damage behavior I did not want in this training fight.
When multiple characters are conscious, Josric normally splits his attacks instead of double-tapping one person.
The principle became: the boss can be unusually durable, but the damage still has to respect the level of the party.

entries.name: How the Finale Changed
entries: I wanted the finale to call back to the rest of the course, so Josric is joined by Book Mimics and class-themed versions of himself.
I staged those extra enemies instead of dropping everything onto the board at once.
The later waves are also a pressure valve. If the party is already struggling, I can hold one back without changing Josric's numbers in the middle of combat.
The most important rule is that defeating Josric ends the exam immediately. The other creatures are complications, not the real objective.
That means a party that recognizes the objective can shorten the fight. That is not a loophole. It is exactly the kind of decision the course is supposed to teach.
Simulated playtesting pushed Josric upward in durability and from one Arcane Burst to two. One Burst made him too passive. Lower hit points made him disappear too quickly.

entries.name: Why the Rooms Look the Same
entries: The repeated library is not just a convenient map trick. It is part of the adventure's identity.
The rooms are different spaces in the world, but they have the same architecture and the same familiar landmarks. Only the pieces needed for the current lesson change.
I want the players to notice the repetition. Opening another door and seeing almost the same library again should become part of both the joke and the unease.

entries.name: Pacing
entries: I was designing for about three hours, but I eventually decided that exactly three hours is not the goal.
If a sharp group finishes thirty minutes early, they earned that.
I do not want to make a puzzle harder, secretly add more hit points, or insert filler because the players are doing well.
The Librarian and Teamwork rooms are optional pacing controls. The hidden number of Teamwork door pairs gives me another way to adjust time without the players seeing the adjustment.

entries.name: What I Learned Making It
entries: Most of the adventure improved when I simplified something.

I cut the history room because I could not make it simple enough. The unlocked door works because it is almost stupidly simple. The teamwork room got better when I removed machinery. The Mirror Gallery got better when I stopped protecting the Echoes from the obvious idea of attacking the mirrors.
I also learned that a room does not need to last a certain number of minutes to justify being there.
I would rather have a player make me say 'that works' than spend ten minutes trying to force them toward my answer.

entries.name: Who Josric Became
entries: Once I settled on Josric instead of Thomage, I wanted him to feel like a real person instead of just the wizard waiting at the end of the dungeon.

I made him a human in his late fifties: old enough to have had a real academic career after the classmates who laughed at his idea, but young and energetic enough that this course still feels like something he has been actively trying to prove rather than an old man's unfinished obsession.
I picture him dressed like a successful professor who actually works in his clothes—formal academic coat, practical layers underneath, too many pockets, ink on his fingers, chalk on his sleeve.

The voice matters almost as much as the clothes. He should sound professorial and a little theatrical, but never like a villain. The thing underneath everything is enthusiasm. He genuinely wants the students to succeed, and clever solutions excite him even when they ruin the answer he expected.

entries.name: For You, Grayson
entries: If you ever run this, change whatever you want.
Change monsters. Replace rooms. Rewrite puzzles. Add the history room if you can make it work. Change Josric if you have a better idea.
The part I hope you keep is the idea underneath it: give the players interesting problems and respect their solutions.
If somebody does something you never considered and it makes sense, that is usually the adventure working.
These notes are not rules. They are what I was thinking when I made this. If you improve something, that does not make it less mine. It makes it ours.

entries.name: Legacy Note
entries: This was not the first adventure I ever wrote. I wrote adventures back in the 1990s, but I never got to run them.
This is the first fully homebrew/original adventure I built with the intention of actually bringing it to the table myself.
After I run it for the first time, I want this archive updated with what actually happened: what the players did, what worked, what failed, what surprised me, and what I changed afterward.
Once that first session has actually happened, this note should be updated to say that it was the first fully homebrew/original adventure I actually brought to the table.

trait.name: Published Chassis
entries: Use the published Juvenile Mimic as the base creature. This course version uses maximum hit points and adds the normal Mimic's Adhesive behavior.

trait.name: False Appearance
entries: While motionless in object form, the mimic is indistinguishable from an ordinary book.

trait.name: Spider Climb
entries: The mimic can climb difficult surfaces, including ceilings, without making an ability check.

trait.name: Adhesive
entries: The mimic adheres to a creature that touches it. A Huge or smaller creature adhered to the mimic is grappled (escape DC 13), and ability checks made to escape this grapple have disadvantage.

action.name: Bite
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 3} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}1 piercing damage plus {@damage 1d4} acid damage.

action.name: Shape-Shift
entries: The mimic changes between its amorphous form and a Tiny book-shaped object. Its statistics do not change.

trait.name: Josric's Reflection
entries: This creature looks like Josric Pickle reimagined through the class role represented by this card. It is not linked to a physical mirror.

trait.name: Training Restraint
entries: The echo does not attack an unconscious creature.

trait.name: Arcane Shield (1/Encounter)
entries: When an attack would hit the echo, it can use its reaction to gain +3 AC against that attack, potentially causing it to miss.

action.name: Arcane Burst
entries: {@atk rs} {@hit 4} to hit, range 120 ft., one target. {@h}{@damage 1d10 + 2} force damage.
